newsitem.title: USA: British retail sales underline economic strength.
newsitem.headline: British retail sales underline economic strength.

text.p: British retail sales, a key indicator of consumer confidence, rose 0.3 percent in March from February, the government said Wednesday, consolidating signs of a strong economy enjoying low inflation and falling unemployment.
Official figures showed retail sales in March rose 4.0 percent over March 1996, compared with 4.3 percent in February. The data were in line with analysts' expectations.

"(The consumer sector) is only likely to get stronger through the year as we see building society pay-outs, house prices still strong and inflation coming down, boosting real incomes," said economist Adrian Schmit of Chase.
The figures were further evidence of strength in the economy and underlined claims by the ruling Conservatives, facing an uphill battle in a May 1 election, that Britain is booming.
But many economists believe the next government will have to raise interest rates -- currently at 6.0 percent -- shortly after the election to prevent the economy overheating.
"Risks remain for a faster pick-up in spending than currently anticipated," said Bank of America analyst Jeremy Hawkins.
Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke has resisted pressure by Bank of England Governor Eddie George to raise interest rates by a quarter percentage point ahead of the election.

The data were released as an opinion poll showed a dramatic fall in the lead enjoyed by the opposition Labour Party, who had looked set to sweep back to power after 18 years in the political wilderness.
The ICM poll showed Labour's lead had shrunk from 14 to just five points, the first time the opposition's advantage has fallen to single figures since November 1993.
